[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Unsupervised Learning: K-Means, DBSCAN, and Hierarchical Clustering"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Unsupervised learning is a branch of machine learning where algorithms are applied to unlabeled data. The primary goal is to discover hidden patterns, inherent groupings, or data structures without human intervention. Clustering is one of the most common unsupervised tasks, aiming to partition a dataset into groups (clusters) such that data points in the same group are more similar to each other than to those in other groups."},{"order":3,"type":"heading","text":"1. K-Means Clustering"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"K-Means is a centroid-based algorithm that partitions data into 'k' distinct clusters. It iteratively updates the cluster centers (centroids) to minimize the within-cluster sum of squares, also known as inertia."},{"order":5,"type":"subheading","text":"K-Means Python Implementation"},{"order":6,"type":"code","text":"from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
import numpy as np

# Sample dataset
X = np.array([[1, 2], [1, 4], [1, 0],
              [4, 2], [4, 4], [4, 0]])

# Initialize KMeans with 2 clusters
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=2, random_state=0, n_init=10)
kmeans.fit(X)

# Predict clusters and find centroids
labels = kmeans.labels_
centroids = kmeans.cluster_centers_
print("Labels:", labels)
print("Centroids:", centroids)"},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Pros: Computationally fast for large datasets; scales well."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Cons: Requires the user to pre-define the number of clusters (k); sensitive to outliers and initial centroid placement."},{"order":9,"type":"heading","text":"2. DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise)"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"DBSCAN views clusters as areas of high density separated by areas of low density. Due to this design, it can discover clusters of arbitrary shapes and is exceptionally robust to outliers, classifying them as noise."},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"DBSCAN Python Implementation"},{"order":12,"type":"code","text":"from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[1, 2], [2, 2], [2, 3],
              [8, 7], [8, 8], [25, 80]])

# eps defines maximum distance, min_samples defines density threshold
dbscan = DBSCAN(eps=3.0, min_samples=2)
dbscan.fit(X)

print("Cluster Labels:", dbscan.labels_)"},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Pros: Does not require specifying the number of clusters beforehand; robust to outliers and identifies arbitrary cluster shapes."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Cons: Struggles with datasets containing widely varying densities; sensitive to hyperparameter tuning (eps and min_samples)."},{"order":15,"type":"heading","text":"3. Hierarchical Clustering"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"Hierarchical clustering builds a tree of clusters. It is typically divided into two approaches: Agglomerative (bottom-up, where each data point starts in its own cluster and pairs are merged) and Divisive (top-down, where all data points start in one cluster and are recursively split)."},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Agglomerative Clustering Python Implementation"},{"order":18,"type":"code","text":"from sklearn.cluster import AgglomerativeClustering
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[1, 2], [1, 4], [1, 0],
              [4, 2], [4, 4], [4, 0]])

# Initialize Agglomerative Clustering
hierarchical = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=2, metric='euclidean', linkage='ward')
hierarchical.fit(X)

print("Cluster Labels:", hierarchical.labels_)"},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Pros: Produces a hierarchical tree (dendrogram) which aids in visualizing and selecting the optimal number of clusters."},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Cons: Computationally expensive for large datasets with high time complexity."},{"order":21,"type":"heading","text":"Summary & Comparison"},{"order":22,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use K-Means when the number of clusters is known and clusters are roughly spherical and evenly sized."},{"order":23,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use DBSCAN when dealing with complex geometric shapes, noise, and unknown cluster counts."},{"order":24,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use Hierarchical Clustering when a dendrogram is needed for analysis and dataset size is manageable."}]
